Section 6 is for SIMPLIFIED single-line pipeline drawings, not detailed views. A pipe is shown by a Type A line on its centre-line, whatever its diameter. Dimensions follow AS 1100.101. Nominal diameter may be shown as DN, and wall thickness on the line. Lengths start from the outer faces of pipe ends or flanges, or the centre of the joint. Bent pipes are dimensioned centre-line to centre-line; the functional angle is shown, and 90 degrees is not. Levels refer to the pipe centre. Line types A, B, G, K are defined in AS 1100.101 (body not on file).

Crossings without a connection do not interrupt the line of the hidden pipe. A permanent junction is a dot five times the line thickness (agrees with ISO 6412). Adjoining apparatus is outlined in Type K lines. Flow direction is an arrow on the pipe or beside a valve symbol. Line types A, B, G, K are defined in AS 1100.101 (body not on file).

Flanges in simplified drawings are Type A lines: two concentric circles in the front view, one stroke for a single flange in side view, two strokes for a pair. Flange holes may be shown as crosses on their centre-lines, one per hole.
items.check: manual; relevant to piping layouts, not to detailed expansion joint views

items.says: Isometric pipeline drawings: coordinate axes per Fig 6.12; deviations from the axes shown with hatched auxiliary planes; centre-line to centre-line dimensions; double dimensions put the second in brackets; points can carry reference numbers (hidden ones in brackets); a continuing drawing gets a note such as 'continued on drawing x'; symbols are drawn isometrically; valve actuators only where position or type matters; cones show nominal sizes above the symbol.

Springs are normally drawn in conventional representation (Table 7.1). Particulars to state depend on the type: helical springs give active coils plus end coils, free length, diameter (outside, mean or inside), section shape and end details; leaf springs give free centres, width and length of each leaf; cup and spiral springs have their own lists.

Splines: shown by symbol and designation near the feature; a true representation with all details is generally avoided. Conventional representation per Table 9.1: root and tooth lines Type B outside the axial section, root surface Type A in the axial section, pitch surface Type G for involute splines. Line types A, B, G, K are defined in AS 1100.101 (body not on file).

Rolling bearings: conventional representation with all features in Type A lines. Where the exact outline matters, draw the true cross-section with an upright cross in the centre. Line types A, B, G, K are defined in AS 1100.101 (body not on file).

Seals (rotating shaft type): general representation is a square with a free-standing diagonal cross centred in it (the cross does not touch the square). Add an arrowhead to the cross only if the sealing direction matters. For exact contour, draw the true cross-section with the diagonal cross centred and not touching it.
items.check: manual; this is shaft-seal representation, not expansion joint seals

items.says: Knurling on a cylindrical feature is shown by a few Type B lines. The feature diameter is the dimension before knurling unless the teeth diameter, pitch or knurl type and grade is stated. Line types A, B, G, K are defined in AS 1100.101 (body not on file).

items.clause: AS 1100.201 App B (informative) B1 to B10
items.says: Castings: a casting drawing should show the casting information, surfaces to be machined and allowances, special requirements and pattern marks. Basic dimensions are for the raw casting before machining. There are 14 tolerance grades, CT3 to CT16. The tolerance zone is symmetric about the basic dimension unless agreed otherwise. Mismatch must lie within the table limit. Dimensions needing other tolerances are toleranced individually; wall thickness tolerance is specified to suit the casting.

General application of Ra values (micrometres), in our own words. 25: very rough, sand casting, torch or saw cutting, rough forgings; unmachined clearance areas. 12.5: very rough, heavy cuts and coarse feeds; clearance areas. 6.3: coarse production surface where tool marks are not objectionable; natural surfaces of forgings, extrusions, rolled surfaces. 3.2: the roughest surface recommended for parts under load, vibration and high stress; medium commercial machine finish; fine for slow, lightly loaded bearing surfaces, not for fast shafts or severe vibration. 1.6: good machine finish under controlled production, for close fits and stressed parts except fast shafts. 0.8: high-grade machine finish needing close control; costs rise rapidly below it. 0.4: high quality, fine grinding or lapping, where smoothness is of primary importance. 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025: very fine to precision gauge finishes, specified only when design makes it mandatory because cost is very high.
items.check: none (guidance). An advisory could flag a very fine Ra (0.4 or finer) on a general arrangement drawing, for a person to look at

items.says: Surface texture symbols: basic symbol is a V with the long leg at 60 degrees to the horizontal, touching the line that represents the surface. With a bar across the top (a triangle) machining is mandatory; with a circle in the V, material removal is not permitted; a horizontal extension on the long leg carries extra indications. Size follows the lettering height h: h 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm gives 1.4h of 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20, 28; 2h of 5, 7, 10, 14, 20, 28, 40; 2.8h of 7, 10, 14, 20, 28, 40, 56 (some rounded up).
items.check: manual; the symbol geometry check is a later task

items.says: The Ra value sits above the symbol (or above the extension line). One value is the maximum; with two values, the maximum is above the minimum. Variants: any production method, machining required, no machining.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Layout of the symbol's indications: a = Ra in micrometres; b = production method, treatment or coating; c = cut-off (sampling length) in millimetres; d = lay; e = machining allowance in millimetres; f = waviness; g = other roughness values in brackets. Items b to g only when required.

items.says: Lay symbols: = parallel to the plane of projection, perpendicular (an upturned T), X crossed in two slant directions, M multi-directional, C approximately circular about the centre, R approximately radial. Each is written beside the symbol.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Examples: production process in words above the extension (MILL); cut-off value below it (2.5); machining allowance to the left of the symbol (5); waviness as height then spacing (0.005 - 5); pre- and post-treatment shown with two symbols (one to a line, one to a Type J line for the treated surface). Table 3.3 lists preferred maximum waviness heights from 0.0005 up to 0.80 mm.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Symbols and their inscriptions are read from the bottom or the right-hand side of the drawing. The symbol points from outside the surface to the line representing it, or to a projection line, and is used once per surface, preferably on the view carrying the dimension that defines it.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Substitute symbols: define what a bare symbol means near the view or title block ('ALL OVER', 'ALL OVER EXCEPT WHERE OTHERWISE INDICATED', or a substitute symbol equal to a symbol with a value). Table 3.4: a value with the V (removal optional), with the bar (obligatory), or with the circle (prohibited), and the two-value form. Table 3.5 gives examples of added indications: milled, cut-off 2.5, perpendicular lay, 2 mm machining allowance, Rz 0.4 in brackets, waviness 0.01 - 5.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Centre hole symbol: two lines at 60 degrees, size from the lettering height (h 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 with line thickness 0.35, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.0). Centre hole required on the finished part: symbol on the end of the centre-line pointing in; must not exist: the symbol is turned the other way. A designation is added: AS 1913 then the drill type, pilot diameter / countersink diameter (for example B 2.5/8).

items.says: Conventional representation of springs: leaf (semi-elliptic, with eyelets, with centre band), helical compression (cylindrical round or square section, conical), tension, torsion, cup and spiral springs, each shown as a sectioned view or a diagrammatic zigzag view.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Splines (straight-sided and involute): shaft, hub and spline joint each drawn as in the table; root and tooth lines Type B in the end view, root surface Type A in the axial section, pitch surface Type G for involute. Tool runout may be an oblique line or a radius; one or two teeth may be drawn with a Type A line to show tooth position.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Rolling bearings: Method A a simple rectangle with a plus sign (general); Method B shows the force type: radial transmission (a rectangle with a short horizontal stroke or a dashed element), axial (a rectangle with a vertical stroke), angular (a rectangle with a diagonal stroke). All Type A lines. For the exact contour, draw the true cross-section with an upright cross in the centre.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Seals: general representation is a square with a free-standing diagonal cross; an arrowhead on the cross shows the sealing direction. Detailed representation builds from elements (a straight line for the static element, a diagonal line for the dynamic lip, short strokes for dust lips and wipers, T over U for contactless seals); Table 11.2 matches seals subject to rotation or translation; Table 11.4 shows labyrinth seals as a T inside a U. These are shaft and rod seals, not expansion joint seals.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Knurling: straight knurling is shown by a few short lines parallel to the axis; diamond knurling by two sets of lines at 30 degrees to the axis, whatever the knurl angle. Type B lines.

items.says: Pipeline figures 6.1 to 6.24, Appendix A Figs A1 and A2, and Appendix B Figs B1 to B4 and Tables B1 to B3. (Section 8 gear figures read 14/11/2026.)

Gears are normally drawn in conventional representation (teeth are not drawn). Terms follow AS 2075 (not on file). Spur, helical, straight bevel, spiral bevel and hypoid forms each have a conventional representation (Table 8.x) and a data summary.

Spur gears are drawn conventionally: the teeth are not drawn. The outside diameter is a continuous line, the pitch circle a thin chain line, the root circle a thin line in the end view; a sectioned side view shows the hub. A gear tooth data block sits beside the view. Essential data (marked with an asterisk) for a spur gear: number of teeth, module (or diametral pitch), pressure angle, pitch diameter, tooth thickness, minimum whole depth, working depth, and class of gear with its standard. Other data: base circle diameter, maximum profile error, accumulated pitch error, adjacent pitch error, tooth alignment error, measurement over rollers and roller diameter, chordal height and chordal tooth thickness. Terms follow AS 2075 (not on file).
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

spur_essential_data: class of gear and relevant standard

items.says: Helical gears are drawn the same way as spur gears. Tooth data adds: lead (right or left hand), helix angle, transverse circular pitch, normal pressure angle, normal arc thickness at pitch line, measuring ball diameter and measurement over balls, maximum lead error, maximum pitch circle diameter runout (FIM relative to a datum X), normal chordal tooth thickness. Crossed helical gears were previously called spiral gears.
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

helical_extra_data: normal arc thickness at pitch line

items.says: Bevel gears: the drawing shows a half-section with the pitch cone and root cone angles (xx degrees xx minutes), the outside tip diameter as a reference, the mounting distance, and the axis of the mating gear or pinion. A gear tooth data table lists, for straight bevel gears: number of teeth, diametral pitch, pitch diameter, shaft angle, working depth, pressure angle, whole depth, root angle, part number of the mating gear, its number of teeth, backlash on the specified mounting, chordal thickness, tooth caliper settings, chordal height, class of gear. Spiral bevel gears replace root angle with hand of spiral and add a summary number (cutter and machine details go on a summary sheet referred to on the drawing). Hypoid pinions add the offset above or below the centre-line, the face angle and the thrust surface (design choice).
items.source: figure or table, read from page images 14/11/2026

items.says: Conventional representation of gears: a straight rack is drawn full length as a plain rectangle (single teeth are drawn with dimensions to show the limits of the toothed portion; the root surface may be a Type B thin line); a cylindrical spur gear is a circle outline with pitch circle and a section; one or more teeth may be drawn to show orientation against another feature such as a keyway; single helical teeth show the helix direction as short diagonal lines on the lower face (right hand), double helical as a V of lines; straight bevel, spiral and hypoid bevels show the cone outlines; worm wheel and worm have their own outlines; gear pairs (double helical, internal spur, rack and pinion, crossed axes, straight bevel, hypoid, worm gearing) show both members, and circles may be replaced by ellipses for clarity. The hand of a spiral shows on the gear and the pinion is the opposite hand.
